﴿By the night when it covers﴾: i.e., it covers over. The object is omitted, and it is the sun, according to His saying: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾, or the day, according to His saying: ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], or everything that the night conceals. ﴿By the day when it appears﴾: i.e., it shows itself and becomes clear. The day is from the rising of the sun, and the day (in the broader sense) is from the rising of dawn. ﴿And by He who created the male and the female﴾: "mā" here means "man" (the one who), and what is meant is God, Exalted is He. He shifted from "man" to "mā" to indicate the attribute, as if He said: "By the Power that created the male and the female." It was also said that "mā" is a maṣdariyya (verbal-noun particle). **﴿As for him who gives⁠﴾**, i.e., gives his wealth in zakat, charity and the like; or gives God's rights through obedience to Him in all matters and is mindful of God. **﴿And affirms the best⁠﴾**, i.e., the good quality, which is Islam; for this reason some have expressed it as "there is no god but God." Or it means the good reward, which is Paradise. It has been said that it means reward and recompense in general, and it has been said that it means the replacement for what is spent. **﴿We will ease him toward ease⁠﴾**, i.e., We will prepare him for the easy path, which is doing good deeds and abandoning evil deeds. The opposite of that is His facilitating for him the hard path (al-'usra). From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Act, for each is made easy for that for which he was created," meaning God prepares him for what He has decreed for him and makes it easy for him to do good or evil.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 92, verse 8–10:

﴿As for he who is niggardly and considers himself self-sufficient﴾. That is, he is niggardly with his wealth or with obedience to God in general, and the verse can bear both meanings, because it stands in contrast to "gives" (aʿṭā), just as "considers himself self-sufficient" (istaghnā) stands in contrast to "is godfearing" (ittaqā). Likewise, "denies the best" (kadhdhaba bil-ḥusnā) stands in contrast to "affirms the best" (ṣaddaqa bil-ḥusnā), and ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ stands in contrast to ﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾. The meaning of "considers himself self-sufficient" (istaghnā) is that he considers himself independent of God, so he does not obey Him, and he considers himself self-sufficient through this world, independent of the Hereafter.

The verse of praise was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, because he spent his wealth seeking God's pleasure, and he used to buy the slaves who had embraced Islam and free them. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah, but this is weak, because the surah is Meccan, and Abu al-Dahdah only embraced Islam in Medina. It has also been said that the verse of blame was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, but this is weak because of His saying: ﴿So We will ease him toward hardship﴾, and Abu Sufyan embraced Islam after that.

This is a Qur'anic quotation, so I render the ﴿ ﴾ markers and translate its meaning inside them.

﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls to ruin.﴾ This is a negation, or a question in the sense of denial. The scholars differed over the meaning of "tarrada" (to fall to ruin) in four opinions. The first: "tarrada" means "halaka" (he perished); it is derived from "al-radaa" (ruin), which is death. Or "tarrada" means he fell into the grave; or he fell into Jahannam (Hellfire); or "tarrada" means he was wrapped in his shroud, from "al-ridaa" (the cloak).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 92, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance﴾, meaning: the explanation of good and evil. The intended sense is not guidance in the sense of direction (al-irshad), according to the Ash'aris, unlike the Mu'tazilites.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 92, verses 14–15:

﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes fiercely﴾ — this is an address from Allah, or from the Prophet (ﷺ), with the implied sense: "Say..." ﴿None will enter it except the most wretched﴾. The Murji'ah (the Murji'ah, a theological school holding that faith is essentially affirmation and that sin does not harm one who believes) used this verse as evidence that only disbelievers will enter the Fire, based on His saying: ﴿who denied and turned away﴾.

The scholars interpreted it in three ways. The first: the meaning is that none will burn in it forever (khulud, i.e., eternal abiding) except the most wretched. The second: He meant a specific Fire. The third: by "the most wretched" He meant a particular disbeliever, namely Abu Jahl and Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and He contrasted with him "the most pious," namely Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). The statement was thus given in the form of specific praise and blame, not in the form of a general announcement.

The Qur'anic verses are between ﴿ ﴾ markers. Translating faithfully:

﴿Who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾ — the verb ﴿yatazakka﴾ may mean from paying zakat (zakah, obligatory almsgiving) or from zakat itself; that is, he becomes pure (zakiyy) before God, or he purifies himself from his sins. This verb is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿yu'ti māluhu﴾ or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in it.

﴿And none has a favour upon him that is to be repaid﴾ — meaning he does not do good as recompense for a blessing bestowed upon him by anyone in the past; rather, he does it from the outset, purely for the sake of God's Face. It was also said: the meaning is that he does not seek a return from anyone in the future for what he does. The first view is more apparent, and it is supported by what is narrated: that the reason for the revelation of the verse is that when Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) freed Bilal, the Quraysh said: "Bilal had a prior favour upon him," so God negated their claim.

﴿Except the seeking of the Face of his Lord﴾ — this is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati').

﴿And he is surely going to be well-pleased﴾ — a promise that God will make him content in the Hereafter.
